one_liner: Bitstream-parallel text-processing framework whose LLVM-JIT'd SIMD kernel beat a simdutf CLI wrapper on UTF-16 validation.
what_it_does: Parabix is a compiler framework, not a library you link: it transposes byte/char streams into parallel bitstreams and JIT-compiles a kernel pipeline with LLVM at build/run time. It ships tools built on the framework (icgrep, wc, base64, transcoders, xml) but no UTF-16 validator; the tools/utf16validate CLI benchmarked here is a student-added tool patched into an older Parabix commit and is absent from this GitHub mirror. There is no stable public API to call — using it means writing pipeline/kernel code against Parabix's builder classes and building the whole framework with its LLVM/Boost/Z3 toolchain.
how_it_is_fast: Core technique is Cameron et al.'s parallel bit-stream method: input is transposed (s2p) into 8/16 bitstreams, each holding one bit-position across the whole buffer, turning per-character branching into bitwise AND/OR/shift ops across a full register width, plus optional multicore pipeline parallelism (--thread-num). On this specific benchmark part of the apparent win is a process/I-O gap rather than kernel speed: Parabix streams the file through ReadSourceKernel while the simdutf wrapper CLI reads the whole file into a std::vector via ifstream before validating; the benchmark authors' own methodology doc says I/O is not equalized between the two.
when_to_use: Building a new streaming text pipeline (regex search, XML parsing, transcoding) where adopting the whole Parabix framework is acceptable, not just linking a validator
Multi-stage text transforms where replacing many per-character branches with bitwise ops across a full register/vector width is the goal (icgrep-style regex matching)
Research or teaching on bit-parallel SIMD algorithms and LLVM JIT code generation
Environments that can carry an LLVM 5+/Boost 1.61+/Z3/CMake toolchain at both build and run time
Workloads that also want multicore pipeline parallelism (thread-num > 1) inside the same kernel model
when_not_to_use: You need a small, embeddable UTF-8/UTF-16 validator with a stable C/C++ API — no such component exists in this mirror; use simdutf directly
Startup latency matters: Parabix's LLVM JIT pipeline load adds ~0.019s fixed overhead per process vs ~0.002s for simdutf, dominating small-input timings
You need permissive licensing — Parabix/icgrep is OSL-3.0 (strong copyleft), unlike simdutf's permissive license
You need an actively maintained project — no commits on this mirror since 2021-08-10
You need UTF-8 rather than UTF-16 — this benchmark and the validator it measures are UTF-16LE only

integration.dependencies: LLVM 5+ (JIT backend), Boost 1.61+, Z3 theorem prover, CMake 2.8+
integration.min_toolchain: C++14; benchmark used Homebrew LLVM 16.0.6 as the JIT backend under Apple clang 21
integration.platforms: x86-64 and aarch64 exercised by the benchmark (Apple M1 native; x86-64 via QEMU); source tree also has NVPTX/CUDA kernel code (editd GPU kernel, NVPTXDriver.h) that this benchmark does not exercise
integration.thread_safety: not documented in README; kernels expose a --thread-num pipeline-parallelism option, but no stated guarantee about concurrent use of a single pipeline instance
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: not an API-level drop-in for simdutf; it is a separate framework/CLI (and the specific validator tool isn't even present in this GitHub mirror), requiring an LLVM JIT toolchain rather than linking a small library

gotchas: The benchmarked tools/utf16validate isn't in this GitHub mirror; it's added by a third-party patch to Parabix commit f0369dd pulled from the SFU GitLab, and that commit postdates this mirror's last sync (2021-08-10)

Fixed per-process overhead (~0.019s, mostly LLVM JIT pipeline load) is roughly 9x simdutf's (~0.002s) — raw wall-clock throughput on small inputs is dominated by this, use the benchmark's overhead-adjusted numbers instead

GitHub reports this repo's license as NOASSERTION even though the README and OSL3.0.txt/LLVM-LICENSE.txt in the tree declare OSL-3.0 for Parabix code and the LLVM Release License for vendored LLVM files
This is a read-only mirror: it does not accept GitHub pull requests; patches go to an SFU GitLab research repo instead
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued UTF-8 siblings (ada-url/idna, simdutf8, xutf, SimdUnicode, utf8_range) target UTF-16, so there's no direct sibling for this workload; pick Parabix over building your own UTF-16 path only if you're already adopting its whole bit-parallel framework for other text processing, not for a standalone validator.
verified_claims_summary: On valid UTF-16LE corpora (128/256 MiB, single thread, Apple M1, median of 7 runs), a third-party benchmark measured Parabix's SIMD kernel at 2900-3760 MiB/s raw (5075-5205 MiB/s overhead-adjusted) against a simdutf v9.0.0 CLI wrapper (clang -O3 -std=c++17) at 1824-2532 MiB/s raw (1883-2600 MiB/s adjusted) -- about 1.18-2.0x raw and 2.0-2.7x adjusted -- but the simdutf wrapper reads the whole file into memory before validating while Parabix streams it, so part of the gap reflects I/O handling rather than the validation kernels.
status_note: Abandoned on this mirror since 2021-08-10 (no evidence in this session of active development elsewhere) and usability is mixed: it's a research framework with no stable API, requiring a full LLVM/Boost/Z3 build toolchain rather than a library you can drop in.
